newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenian investment rules keeping foreigners away.
newsitem.headline: Slovenian investment rules keeping foreigners away.

text.p: International investors are threatening to steer clear of Slovenian securities until the central bank eases unpopular regulations that restrict foreign portfolio investment.

"Without fast changes, foreigners will stay away and foreign portfolio investment could remain at a minimum for years," James Oates, director of Eastern & Central European Equities at Union Bank of Switzerland, told Reuters during an investment conference on Friday.
In February, the Bank of Slovenia blocked the inflow of foreign funds by ruling that international investors must open fiduciary accounts at one of Slovenia's banks in order to trade in securities.
Since the central bank decree the Ljubljana stock exchange's blue-chip SBI index has fallen by 17.7 percent while volume has dropped by about 75 percent.
The special accounts have not yet been set up by the banks, but are expected to charge between nine and 15 percent.

"That is too expensive," said Yves Kuhn of Pictet Asset Management in London. "We are being forced to open a fiduciary account because we have already invested close to $20 million in Slovenian securities. But if the conditions do not change, we will place fresh capital elsewhere," Kuhn said.
The Bank of Slovenia repeated on Thursday it had no plans to reform investment rules before 1998 when Slovenia's association agreement with the European Union is due to come into force.
Analysts expect just $17 million of new foreign inflows in the remainder of the end of the year compared with $30 million invested in the six weeks before the central bank ruling.
Oates said central bank intransigence over the fiduciary accounts was just one of several obstacles facing potential investors from abroad.

"The Bank of Slovenia decree is just the most immediate problem. Another problem is that we have been waiting over a year for new securities legislation and that is extremelly disappointing," he said.
Financiers say Slovenia needs to bring in new laws detailing portfolio investment rules and reducing currency restrictions.
At present Slovenian banks have to balance foreign liabilities, including money paid into fiduciary accounts, against foreign assets.

"Slovenia needs to introduce legislation that will differentiate between long-term international investors and those who speculate," said Olivier Descamps, director of the Slovenia country team at the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development.
"The current rules send out the wrong signals to some real stategic investors," he added.
Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek said new laws on securities trading and foreign exchange transactions were among government priorities.
"The two laws have full priority in the government and I hope also in the parliament," Drnovsek said. He gave no details on when the laws would be introduced.
